A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MBR inference and distillation study. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable, and retained content can be matched across appendix moves and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original decoding and self-training experiments, NLP benchmark evaluations, and a human evaluation study in Appendix H.

after.justification: v4 retains those original results and adds linguistic analyses, speculative-decoding and judge-correlation experiments, and Llama-3 distillation results.

M1.justification: Appendix A.6 adds an inference variant combining MBR with speculative decoding and a draft model. The central expected-utility selection rule and iterative DPO procedure remain unchanged; Algorithms 1–2 document these existing procedures.

E1.justification: Both versions use UltraChat, AlpacaEval 2.0, MT-Bench, MMLU, ARC challenge, HellaSwag, and TruthfulQA. The new analyses reuse existing task coverage. The 100-prompt speculative-decoding subset and additional model configurations change experimental settings rather than datasets or task requirements.

E2.justification: Table 3 adds Llama-3-8b-Instruct as an evaluated judge for both BoN and MBR decoding. Appendix G.4 also compares Prometheus and Llama-3-8b-Instruct for distillation. Existing comparisons with beam search, sampling methods, USC, other judges, and Starling-RM are retained.

E3.justification: Existing benchmark protocols and training hyperparameters are retained. Additional studies introduce formatting, lexical-diversity and readability metrics; a 100-sample timing experiment; and first-turn MT-Bench rank-correlation evaluation with 30 candidates, generation temperature 0.7, and GPT-4o temperature 0.5. Llama-3-8b distillation adds another training-model configuration.

E4.justification: v4 substantially broadens supplementary analysis: Appendix A.5 examines formatting, lexical diversity, and readability; A.6 tests acceleration through speculative decoding; A.7 examines agreement with GPT-4o; and G.4 tests distillation with different judges on Llama-3-8b. These address additional questions beyond v1's retained sensitivity, category, length, and preference-pair analyses.

E5.justification: Appendix A.7 adds a statistical procedure averaging three sampled GPT-4o ratings per output and estimating Spearman rank correlations. The existing median-of-three evaluation in Appendix B and Figure 3's standard errors remain unchanged. This does not establish increased repetition of existing experiments; no new training-seed reporting, confidence intervals, or significance tests are provided.

E6.justification: v4 adds substantive findings on linguistic similarity, inference costs, judge agreement, and Llama-3 distillation while retaining existing numerical results. Table 10 reports 59.3 versus 52.9 seconds per generation for vanilla versus speculative MBR. Table 16 reports Llama-3-8b improving from 6.70 to 7.55 or 7.52 after distillation with the two judges. These are newly reported experiments, not performance changes between versions under retained settings.

T1.justification: Appendix I.2 newly supplies the explicit DPO objective in Equation 5 and formalizes construction of the preference dataset, previously described procedurally. Equation 4 restates the existing expected-utility calculation. No new theorem, proof, or substantive theoretical guarantee is added.

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion retain the same central claims: LLM-judge MBR improves instruction following, small judges can supervise larger models, and iterative DPO can recover MBR-level performance with greedy decoding. Additional experiments support these claims without changing their main scope.

C2.justification: New Appendix J explicitly discusses potentially suboptimal consensus choices, stronger reference-free alternatives, utility-model bias and reward hacking, and limits to supervision by weaker judges. Appendix A.7 adds an interpretation concerning GPT-4o bias, while G.4 suggests a possibility of self-improvement. Together these substantially expand the paper's interpretations and applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: v4 adds explicit inference and distillation pseudocode, formal training-objective documentation, a rationale for using 12 distillation candidates, and the draft-model identifier for speculative decoding. Existing prompts, hardware information, and hyperparameter tables are retained; the hyperparameter appendix moves from I to K.

R1.justification: v4 more explicitly credits Yang et al. with MBR-based DPO and identifies iterative repetition as its extension; it also attributes SFT distillation to Finkelstein et al. Both works were already cited in v1. New references to Flesch, Richards, and Leviathan support the added analyses without fundamentally changing the research positioning.

P1.justification: Changes include localized rewrites of the method and related-work passages, standardized Llama naming, updated affiliations, acknowledgements, and new algorithms and limitations appendices. The main section sequence and most existing prose remain intact.

P2.justification: v4 adds compact Tables 8–11 and 16, two algorithm displays, and two rows in Table 3. Existing figures and tables are retained, with modest resizing, relocation, and page reflow, plus the conference header. The overall visual organization remains similar.

improvement.justification: The added diagnostics, Llama-3 distillation comparison, explicit algorithms, clearer attribution, and specific limitations improve scrutiny and understanding of the work while preserving its original evidence. The gains are limited rather than transformative. Appendix J also overstates the unchanged small human study's ability to rule out reward hacking, which tempers the benefit of the expanded limitations discussion.
